problem.title: Design a Scalable Notification Service
problem.prompt: Design a notification service for a social media platform. The service must deliver notifications to users via push (mobile), email, and in-app channels. Notifications are triggered by user events (likes, comments, follows, mentions). The system must be reliable, handle notification preferences, and avoid spamming users.
requirements: Deliver notifications via push (APNs/FCM), email (SMTP/SES), and in-app channels.
Respect per-user notification preferences (enabled/disabled per type and channel).
Deduplicate: do not send duplicate notifications for the same event within a time window.
Batch low-priority notifications (e.g., group 5 likes into one notification).
Prioritize: deliver time-sensitive notifications (e.g., DM, security alert) with low latency.
constraints: 10 million daily active users; peak: 500,000 notification events/second.
Push delivery p99 < 5 seconds after event; email < 1 minute.
In-app notifications must be queryable (paginated history per user).
At-least-once delivery guarantee; tolerate duplicate delivery if deduplicated at receiver.
Support notification expiry (e.g., a 'like' notification older than 24 hours is stale).

stages.learnerPrompt: Break down the core challenges: fanout (one event → many notifications), preference filtering, deduplication, and delivery guarantees. Identify the main components before designing.

referenceMaterial.summary: Main challenges: (1) Fanout — a single event (e.g., a post from a celebrity with 10M followers) generates millions of push notifications. (2) Preference filtering — each recipient has different opt-in/opt-out settings. (3) Reliability — ensure delivery even if a channel (push) is temporarily down. (4) Batching/rate limiting — avoid overwhelming users with dozens of individual notifications.
tradeOffs: Push fanout synchronously: simple but blocks event processing and slows the platform.
Message queue + async workers: decouples notification from event source; preferred pattern.
Write fanout vs read fanout: write fanout (write to each recipient's inbox on event) is simple but expensive for celebrities; read fanout (compute on read) reduces writes but increases read latency.

stages.learnerPrompt: Sketch the architecture. How does an event become a notification? How do you route to the right channel for each user? What ensures delivery?

referenceMaterial.summary: Event → Kafka topic → Notification Service (preference filter + dedup) → Channel Workers (push/email/in-app).
approachSteps: 1. Platform emits a domain event (e.g., UserLikedPost{postId, actorId, recipientId}) to Kafka.
2. Notification Service consumes the event: fetch recipient preferences from a low-latency cache (Redis); if the channel is disabled or event type is muted, drop the event.
3. Deduplication: check a Redis set {recipientId}:{eventType}:{entityId}:{windowHash} with TTL = dedup window (e.g., 1 hour). If key exists, drop; else SET NX and continue.
4. Batching worker: for low-priority types (likes, follows), accumulate events in a Redis sorted set by recipient, flush every 30 seconds, send a single batched notification.
5. Fanout: for high-priority (DM, security), route directly to the channel worker queue.
6. Channel workers: push worker calls APNs/FCM; email worker calls SES; in-app worker writes to a notifications table (sharded by userId) and updates a Redis badge counter.
7. Delivery failure: retry with exponential backoff; after max retries, write to a dead-letter queue for audit.
referenceMaterial.diagramDescription:
[ Business Microservices ] -> [ Notification API Gateway ] -> [ Redis Idempotency Lock ]
                                    |
                                    v
                           [ Kafka Event Queue ]
                                    |
          +-------------------------+-------------------------+
          |                         |                         |
          v                         v                         v
  [ Push Worker Pool ]     [ SMS Worker Pool ]      [ Email Worker Pool ]
  (APNs / FCM)             (Twilio / Vonage)        (SendGrid / Amazon SES)
alternatives: SNS (AWS): managed fan-out to SQS queues per channel. Reduces operational burden; less control over batching logic.
Celery/worker per recipient: simple for low scale; fan-out storm for popular users.
Websocket push for in-app: enables real-time updates without polling; requires persistent connection management.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why separate queues per channel? Why Redis for dedup and preferences vs the primary DB? When would you use read fanout instead of write fanout?

tradeOffs: Separate queues per channel: failures in email delivery do not block push delivery; scaling is independent.
Redis for preferences: avoids DB read on every notification event; stale preference cache (up to TTL) is acceptable — a user muting a notification type will stop receiving after the TTL expires.

Write fanout vs read fanout: Write fanout writes to each follower's queue immediately — O(followers) writes per post. Read fanout computes on read — O(followers) reads per inbox load. Write fanout is faster for notification delivery; read fanout is cheaper for celebrities (99% of followers never check their inbox).
Hybrid: use write fanout for regular users (<10K followers) and read fanout (or dedicated celebrity workers with throttled write) for high-follower accounts.
referenceMaterial.summary: Comprehensive evaluation of multi-channel notification architecture: dedicated channel queues vs unified topics, write fanout vs read fanout, in-memory Redis deduplication, and multi-lane priority tiering.

sections.content:
### What to Focus On
* **Primary Objective**: Architect a resilient, high-volume multi-channel notification engine (Email, SMS, Mobile Push, In-App) capable of dispatching millions of alerts while maintaining strict delivery isolation, idempotency deduplication, and low-latency priority routing.
* **Key Decision Levers**:
  1. **Queue Architecture**: Dedicated Queues per Delivery Channel vs Unified Monolithic Topic.
  2. **Fanout Strategy**: Write Fanout (Push-on-Write) vs Read Fanout (Pull-on-Read) vs Hybrid.
  3. **Deduplication Mechanism**: In-Memory Redis Distributed Idempotency vs Primary Relational DB Unique Constraints.
  4. **Traffic Tiering & Priority**: Multi-Lane Priority Queues (Transactional OTP vs Marketing Blasts).
* **What You Should Be Able to Explain**:
  - Why bundling email, SMS, and push notifications into a single queue causes slow email providers to backpressure and delay real-time SMS one-time passwords (OTPs).
  - How write fanout scales for typical users ($< 5,000$ followers) but causes write amplification crashes for celebrity accounts ($10\text{M}+$ followers), and how hybrid fanout resolves the discrepancy.
  - How distributed Redis idempotency keys prevent duplicate mobile push alerts during worker retries.
  - How to handle third-party carrier rate limits (Twilio, SendGrid, APNs, FCM) without dropping outbound messages.
---

### Structured Decision Breakdown & Rationale

#### 1. Delivery Topology: Dedicated Channel Queues vs Unified Queue
* **Option A: Dedicated Queues per Delivery Channel [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: **Fault Isolation & Independent Scaling**. A massive marketing email blast or slow third-party SMTP server never blocks urgent SMS two-factor authentication codes.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Slightly higher infrastructure operational complexity (managing separate topics/queues for Email, SMS, APNs, and In-App).
  * **When to Choose**: Any production notification engine delivering through multiple channels with differing delivery latencies and carrier rate limits.
* **Option B: Single Unified Notification Queue**
  * **Optimizes For**: Simplicity of deployment (one producer queue, one consumer worker group).
  * **Cost / Downside**: **Head-of-Line Blocking**: Email providers (SendGrid, SES) enforce strict rate limits ($100\text{ emails/sec}$). A marketing email blast of $500,000$ messages fills the queue, stalling real-time login OTP SMS codes for hours.
  * **When to Choose**: Prototypes or applications supporting only a single channel (e.g. email only).
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Dedicated Queues per Delivery Channel**. Channel isolation ensures that third-party rate limits, downstream carrier outages, or worker crashes in one channel cannot degrade or delay other delivery pathways.

#### 2. Fanout Strategy: Write Fanout vs Read Fanout vs Hybrid
* **Option A: Write Fanout (Push-on-Write)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Ultra-fast notification inbox reads ($O(1)$ query from user inbox table).
  * **Cost / Downside**: **Celebrity Write Amplification**: When an account with $50\text{M}$ followers posts an update, the system must write $50\text{M}$ records to the database, exhausting storage IOPS and delaying alerts by hours.
  * **When to Choose**: Systems where all users have a small, bounded number of connections ($< 5,000$).
* **Option B: Read Fanout (Pull-on-Read)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Instant post creation ($O(1)$ write); zero storage amplification.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Slow inbox read latency ($O(K)$ where $K$ is the number of followed users). Every inbox refresh requires querying all followed accounts and sorting in memory.
  * **When to Choose**: Applications where write traffic dwarfs read traffic and users rarely check their inboxes.
* **Option C: Hybrid Fanout (Threshold-Based) [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: The best of both worlds: fast inbox reads for $99.9\%$ of users without celebrity write amplification.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Increased application routing logic to categorize accounts above/below the follower threshold (e.g., $10,000$ followers).
  * **When to Choose**: Large-scale social and community platforms (Twitter/X, Instagram, LinkedIn).
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Hybrid Fanout**. Standard user actions push directly into follower inboxes, while high-follower celebrity updates are merged on-demand during client inbox reads, capping peak write amplification.

#### 3. State Deduplication: Redis In-Memory vs Primary Database Unique Indexes
* **Option A: Redis Distributed Idempotency Key Check [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Sub-millisecond deduplication checks without putting read/write load on the primary relational database.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Requires Redis availability and memory budgeting; keys must have an explicit expiration TTL ($10\text{--}60\text{ minutes}$).
  * **When to Choose**: High-throughput distributed event-driven systems where duplicate network retries occur frequently.
* **Option B: Primary Database Unique Constraint (`UNIQUE(event_id, user_id)`)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Permanent, guaranteed relational consistency.
  * **Cost / Downside**: High database write lock contention; unique constraint violations throw exceptions that require database transaction rollbacks.
  * **When to Choose**: Low-volume systems ($< 100\text{ notifications/sec}$) with strict ACID financial requirements.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Redis In-Memory Deduplication** using `SET key value NX EX 300`. This validates uniqueness atomically in $< 1\text{ ms}$, shielding primary persistent databases from the massive write volume of event retries.

#### 4. Traffic Priority: Multi-Lane Priority Queues vs FIFO
* **Option A: Multi-Lane Priority Queues [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Strict SLA guarantees. Transactional events (Password Reset OTP, Fraud Alerts) are routed to a dedicated high-priority lane with zero queue lag.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Requires separate worker pools and priority arbitration logic.
  * **When to Choose**: Any platform combining security/transactional alerts with promotional marketing messages.
* **Option B: Single First-In First-Out (FIFO) Queue**
  * **Optimizes For**: Simplicity and preservation of chronological order across all notification types.
  * **Cost / Downside**: High-volume marketing campaigns completely starve urgent transactional notifications.
  * **When to Choose**: Internal systems where all notifications have identical business urgency.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Multi-Lane Priority Queues**. Security and transaction notifications are critical for business operations and must never be delayed behind scheduled marketing newsletters.

---

### Decision Comparison Tables

#### Table 1: Channel Delivery Architecture
| Architecture | Isolation Guarantee | Infrastructure Cost | Scale Complexity | Blast Radius on Outage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dedicated Channel Queues** | **High (100% Isolated)** | Moderate | Low (Scale workers per queue) | **Isolated to single channel** |
| **Single Monolithic Queue** | None (Shared buffer) | Low | High (Bottlenecked by slowest channel)| Whole notification system blocked |
| **Topic + Fanout Worker** | High | Moderate | Moderate (Worker routing logic) | Isolated to consumer group |

#### Table 2: Fanout Strategy Matrix
| Metric / Characteristic | Write Fanout (Push) | Read Fanout (Pull) | Hybrid Fanout |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Write Cost on New Post** | $O(N)$ (Writes to all followers) | **$O(1)$ (Single write)** | $O(N)$ for normal, $O(1)$ for VIP |
| **Read Latency on Inbox Open**| **$O(1)$ (Point lookup)** | $O(K)$ (Merge $K$ feeds) | **$O(1)$ (Point lookup + VIP merge)** |
| **Celebrity Scale Vulnerability**| **Severe (Write storm crashes DB)**| None | **None (Handled via pull branch)** |
| **Storage Consumption** | High (Duplicated rows per user) | Minimal | Balanced |
| **Recommended Usage** | Private chats / Small groups | Low-read platforms | **Social networks / Large communities** |

---

### Hidden Assumptions & Edge Realities
1. **Third-Party Carrier Rate Limits**: Providers like Apple APNs, Google FCM, Twilio, and SendGrid enforce strict concurrency and per-second rate limits. Workers must implement token-bucket throttling to stay within carrier quotas.
2. **User Notification Preference Caching**: User preferences (e.g., "Mute marketing emails", "SMS only for security") must be cached in Redis with a 5-to-15 minute TTL; querying the database on every notification event would cripple database read throughput.
3. **At-Least-Once Delivery Reality**: Distributed message brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. The mobile client and notification service must be idempotent: displaying or logging an alert twice must produce the identical user state.

---

### Common Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
* **The Marketing Blackout of Login OTPs**: Placing a 2-million user marketing campaign in the same queue as two-factor authentication (2FA) SMS codes, causing login codes to take 45 minutes to arrive and locking all users out of the application.
* **Push Notification Duplicate Storms**: When a network timeout occurs between your worker and Apple APNs, the worker blindly retries without checking the idempotency key, causing the user's phone to buzz 10 times with the exact same alert.
* **Unbounded Memory Buffers During Carrier Outages**: When Twilio or SendGrid suffers a global outage, workers retry continuously in memory, filling server RAM and causing out-of-memory (OOM) crashes across the entire gateway cluster.
* **Ignoring Delivery Receipts (DLR) Webhooks**: Failing to process carrier delivery status webhooks, leaving broken phone numbers and invalid email addresses in active campaigns and degrading domain sender reputation.

---

### Concrete Implementation Examples & Payloads

#### 1. Notification Ingestion API Request
```http
POST /api/v1/notifications HTTP/1.1
Host: notify.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: idemp_98fa012-45e1-88c9

{
  "recipientUserId": "usr_9981240",
  "templateId": "tmpl_security_login_alert",
  "priority": "HIGH",
  "channels": ["PUSH", "EMAIL"],
  "payload": {
    "ipAddress": "192.0.2.1",
    "location": "San Francisco, CA",
    "device": "Safari on macOS",
    "timestamp": "2026-11-01T07:50:00Z"
  }
}
```

#### 2. Standardized Outbound Event Schema (Kafka / RabbitMQ)
```json
{
  "eventId": "evt_55102a-99bc-4311",
  "idempotencyKey": "idemp_98fa012-45e1-88c9",
  "userId": "usr_9981240",
  "channel": "PUSH",
  "priority": "HIGH",
  "deviceTokens": ["fcm_token_abc123..."],
  "title": "New Login Detected",
  "body": "A new login was recorded from Safari on macOS in San Francisco, CA.",
  "metadata": {
    "actionUrl": "https://example.com/security/sessions",
    "retryCount": 0
  },
  "createdAt": 1793471400000
}
```

#### 3. Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) Quarantined Message
```json
{
  "dlqReason": "CARRIER_RATE_LIMIT_EXHAUSTED",
  "lastStatusCode": 429,
  "carrierName": "Twilio_SMS_Gateway",
  "totalRetries": 3,
  "failedAt": "2026-11-01T07:50:15Z",
  "originalMessage": {
    "eventId": "evt_55102a-99bc-4311",
    "channel": "SMS",
    "recipientPhone": "+14155552671",
    "body": "Your security verification code is 492019."
  }
}
```

stages.learnerPrompt: A celebrity with 5M followers posts a video. Push notifications need to go out within 5 seconds. How does your design handle this fanout burst? What happens if APNs is slow or down?

failureModes: Celebrity fanout: 5M push notifications in 5 seconds = 1M/sec. A single Kafka consumer + push worker cannot keep up. Solution: horizontal scaling of push workers; partition the notifications Kafka topic by userId hash so consumers can parallelize. Precompute follower lists for high-fan-out accounts.

APNs slow: push workers timeout waiting for APNs. Solution: set a short timeout (2 s); if APNs is slow, put undelivered notifications back in the queue with lower priority. Users will receive the push when APNs recovers.
APNs down: retry with exponential backoff up to the notification expiry TTL. After expiry, drop — stale notifications degrade UX more than missing ones.
In-app notification write surge: shard the notifications table by userId; use a write-behind cache (Redis) to absorb burst writes and flush to the DB asynchronously.

stages.learnerPrompt: New requirement: users can now set a 'Do Not Disturb' schedule (e.g., no notifications from 10 PM to 8 AM local time). High-priority notifications (security alerts, DMs) must still be delivered immediately. How do you implement this without blocking the notification pipeline?

approachSteps: 1. Store DND schedules in the user preferences table (start_hour, end_hour, timezone).
2. When a notification is about to be dispatched, check if recipient is in DND window (convert user's local time using stored timezone).
3. If DND active AND notification priority is not 'critical': delay the notification by adding it to a scheduled delivery queue (Redis sorted set keyed by userId, scored by scheduled_delivery_time).
4. A scheduler process polls the sorted set every minute and re-enqueues notifications whose delivery time has passed.
5. If priority is 'critical' (DM, security): bypass DND check and deliver immediately.
tradeOffs: Redis sorted set for delayed delivery: simple, low latency, but Redis is in-memory — persisted scheduled notifications need DB backup for durability.
Per-notification vs batch: check DND per notification at dispatch time. More accurate than batch processing, but adds a Redis lookup per notification.
Timezone accuracy: always store user timezone explicitly — do not infer from IP. Use IANA timezone identifiers.

problem.title: Design a Scalable Notification Service
problem.prompt: Design a notification service for a social media platform. The service must deliver notifications to users via push (mobile), email, and in-app channels. Notifications are triggered by user events (likes, comments, follows, mentions). The system must be reliable, handle notification preferences, and avoid spamming users.
requirements: Deliver notifications via push (APNs/FCM), email (SMTP/SES), and in-app channels.
Respect per-user notification preferences (enabled/disabled per type and channel).
Deduplicate: do not send duplicate notifications for the same event within a time window.
Batch low-priority notifications (e.g., group 5 likes into one notification).
Prioritize: deliver time-sensitive notifications (e.g., DM, security alert) with low latency.
constraints: 10 million daily active users; peak: 500,000 notification events/second.
Push delivery p99 < 5 seconds after event; email < 1 minute.
In-app notifications must be queryable (paginated history per user).
At-least-once delivery guarantee; tolerate duplicate delivery if deduplicated at receiver.

concept.whyItMatters: A notification service is deceptively complex at scale: it must fan out a single event to millions of users, respect per-user preferences, deduplicate retries, and deliver across heterogeneous channels (push, email, SMS, in-app) — all within strict latency SLAs and without spamming users.
whenToUse: Event-driven platforms where user actions (likes, mentions, follows, purchases) trigger cross-channel alerts.
Applications with multi-channel delivery requirements (push, email, SMS, in-app) each with different latency and reliability contracts.
Systems handling high-follower celebrity or viral content where write fanout would amplify to millions of rows per event.
whenNotToUse: Simple transactional systems with a single delivery channel and low user count where a synchronous email send suffices.
Internal tooling where delivery SLAs and deduplication complexity are unnecessary overhead.
keyPoints: Fan-out must be asynchronous: synchronous fanout on the event source blocks the platform and cannot scale to 500,000 events/sec.
Dedicated queues per channel (push, email, SMS, in-app) provide fault isolation — a slow SMTP provider cannot block APNs push delivery.
Redis SETNX with TTL provides sub-millisecond idempotency checks without putting duplicate-key write load on the primary database.
Hybrid fanout (write for regular users, read-merge for celebrities) prevents write amplification storms on high-follower accounts.
At-least-once delivery from message brokers requires idempotent consumers — the notification service must tolerate and suppress duplicate events.

terms.definition: On each new event, immediately write a notification record to each follower's inbox — O(followers) writes per event.
Compute a user's notification inbox on-demand by merging events from all followed accounts — O(followed accounts) reads per inbox open.
A unique identifier per notification event stored in Redis with SETNX; duplicate deliveries are suppressed if the key already exists.
A separate queue where messages that exceed maximum retry attempts are moved for manual inspection or alerting, preventing silent message loss.
Apple Push Notification Service and Firebase Cloud Messaging — the platform-managed push delivery gateways for iOS and Android devices.

tradeOffs.pro: Write fanout delivers O(1) inbox reads; read fanout avoids O(followers) writes per celebrity post.
tradeOffs.con: Write fanout causes catastrophic write amplification for high-follower accounts; read fanout increases inbox load latency.

tradeOffs.factor: Dedicated Channel Queues vs Unified Queue
tradeOffs.pro: Dedicated queues isolate channel failures and allow independent scaling of push vs email workers.
tradeOffs.con: Unified queues are simpler to operate but risk head-of-line blocking when one channel is slow.

tradeOffs.factor: Redis Deduplication vs DB Unique Constraint
tradeOffs.pro: Redis SETNX checks complete in sub-millisecond with no DB write lock contention.
tradeOffs.con: Redis deduplication is not durable — a Redis restart during a TTL window could allow a brief duplicate window.

failureModes.name: Celebrity Write Amplification Storm
failureModes.description: A high-follower account event triggers millions of write-fanout inbox writes, exhausting database IOPS and delaying notification delivery by hours.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply hybrid fanout: threshold at ~10K followers. Use write fanout below threshold; switch to read-merge fanout (or throttled background write) above threshold.

failureModes.name: Channel Head-of-Line Blocking
failureModes.description: A marketing email blast of 2 million messages fills a shared queue, causing login OTP SMS codes to queue behind email messages for 45 minutes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use dedicated per-channel queues with independent worker pools and priority lanes for transactional vs promotional traffic.

failureModes.name: Third-Party Carrier Rate Limiting
failureModes.description: APNs, FCM, Twilio, or SendGrid enforce concurrency and per-second rate limits; exceeding them causes silent message drops or HTTP 429 rejections.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement token-bucket throttling per carrier within the channel worker, and back off with exponential retry bounded by the notification TTL.

commonMistakes: Placing OTP SMS notifications and marketing email blasts in the same queue, causing critical transactional messages to stall behind promotional campaigns.
Not setting an expiry (TTL) on delayed notifications — a 'like' notification delivered 24 hours late degrades user experience worse than dropping it.
Ignoring carrier delivery receipt webhooks, leaving invalid device tokens and email addresses in active campaigns and degrading domain reputation.
Retrying APNs failures blindly without an idempotency check, causing duplicate push storms when network timeouts occur mid-delivery.

sections.content:
## Define the Scope & Problem Statement

Design a notification service for a social media platform that delivers notifications via push (APNs/FCM), email (SMTP/SES), and in-app channels. Notifications are triggered by user events (likes, comments, follows, mentions) and must be reliable, preference-aware, and deduplicated.

The central design tension is **fanout at scale**: a single celebrity post can trigger 10M push notifications within seconds. The system must handle this burst asynchronously while maintaining strict per-channel latency SLAs and never duplicating or losing a notification.

## Requirements & Scale Constraints

### Functional Requirements
- Deliver notifications via push (APNs/FCM), email (SMTP/SES), and in-app channels.
- Respect per-user notification preferences (enabled/disabled per type and channel).
- Deduplicate: do not send duplicate notifications for the same event within a time window.
- Batch low-priority notifications (e.g., group 5 likes into one notification).
- Prioritize: deliver time-sensitive notifications (DM, security alert) with low latency.

### Non-Functional Constraints
- 10 million daily active users; peak: 500,000 notification events/second.
- Push delivery p99 < 5 seconds after event; email < 1 minute.
- In-app notifications must be queryable (paginated history per user).
- At-least-once delivery guarantee; tolerate duplicate delivery if deduplicated at receiver.
- Support notification expiry (e.g., a 'like' notification older than 24 hours is stale).

## Capacity Estimation & Sizing

- **Event Ingestion**: 500,000 events/sec peak → ~50 GB/day of raw event data into Kafka (at ~100 bytes/event).
- **Fanout Writes**: Average 50 followers per user = 25M notification writes/sec at peak. Celebrity accounts capped via hybrid fanout.
- **Push Channel**: 10M DAU × 3 notifications/day = 30M push deliveries/day ≈ 350/sec average, 5,000/sec peak.
- **In-App Storage**: 30M notifications/day × 500 bytes = ~15 GB/day. Sharded by userId; 90-day retention = ~1.35 TB.
- **Redis Dedup**: 500K events/sec × 300 bytes key = ~150 MB/sec write rate; at 1-hour TTL, steady-state memory ≈ 540 GB — shard across a Redis cluster.

sections.content:
## Fanout Strategy: Write vs Read vs Hybrid

The fanout model determines how a single event becomes per-recipient notifications:

**Write Fanout (Push-on-Write)**: When an event occurs, immediately write a notification row to each follower's inbox. O(followers) writes per event.
- ✅ O(1) inbox reads — users open their inbox and read pre-computed rows.
- ❌ Celebrity problem: 10M followers × 1 event = 10M writes/event. At 100 events/sec from celebrities, this is 1B writes/sec — catastrophic.

**Read Fanout (Pull-on-Read)**: Store only the event. When a user opens their inbox, fetch and merge events from all followed accounts.
- ✅ O(1) writes per event regardless of follower count.
- ❌ Slow inbox load: merging feeds from 1,000 followed accounts requires 1,000 DB reads per inbox open.

**Hybrid Fanout (Recommended)**: Write fanout for accounts with ≤ 10K followers. Read fanout (or throttled background write) for celebrity accounts above the threshold.
- ✅ Fast reads for 99.9% of users; no write amplification for celebrities.
- Tradeoff: routing logic must categorize accounts and merge celebrity feeds on inbox read.

## Deduplication & Preference Filtering

**Deduplication**: Use Redis `SETNX` with a composite key:
```
dedup:{recipientId}:{eventType}:{entityId}:{windowBucket}
```
Set TTL equal to the dedup window (e.g., 1 hour). If the key exists, drop the notification. This prevents duplicate push alerts when workers retry after network timeouts.

**Preference Filtering**: Cache user preferences (opt-in/opt-out per channel and event type) in Redis with a 5–15 minute TTL. Query the cache before every notification dispatch — do not read from the primary DB on the hot path. Stale cache (up to TTL) is acceptable: a user who mutes a notification type will stop receiving within the TTL window.

## Failure Handling & Graceful Degradation

- **APNs / FCM Slow or Down**: Set a short timeout (2 s) on channel workers. On timeout, re-enqueue with lower priority. Retry with exponential backoff up to the notification TTL; drop after expiry.
- **Redis Dedup Unavailable**: Fail open — allow notification dispatch without dedup check. Log anomaly for review. The mobile client and in-app view should be idempotent and suppress visible duplicates.
- **Kafka Consumer Lag**: Scale out worker pods horizontally. Partition Kafka topics by userId hash to allow parallel consumption. Use consumer group lag alerts to trigger auto-scaling.
- **Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ)**: After max retries, route failed messages to a DLQ. Alert on DLQ depth; manually replay or discard after investigation.

## Final Synthesis & Trade-Off Defense

In a system design interview, conclude by explicitly defending your architectural trade-offs:

- **Dedicated Channel Queues**: Fault isolation is the primary justification. Email provider rate limits must never delay push OTPs. Independent scaling per channel is a secondary benefit.
- **Hybrid Fanout Threshold**: Set at ~10K followers based on the write amplification math. Above the threshold, use read-merge at inbox open time with a Redis sorted-set cache of recent celebrity events.
- **At-Least-Once Delivery**: Accept at-least-once from Kafka. Dedup at the gateway (Redis SETNX) prevents visible duplicates. Mobile clients must handle idempotent notification display.
- **Notification TTL**: Always set an expiry on queued notifications. A 'like' delivered 48 hours late is worse UX than a missed notification — drop gracefully after TTL.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Design a notification service for a social media platform. The service must deliver notifications to users via push (mobile), email, and in-app channels. Notifications are triggered by user events (likes, comments, follows, mentions). The system must be reliable, handle notification preferences, and avoid spamming users.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Kafka Event Bus applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Email Worker Pool.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Celebrity fanout: 5M push notifications in 5 seconds = 1M/sec. A single Kafka consumer + push worker cannot keep up. Solution: horizontal scaling of push workers; partition the notifications Kafka topic by userId hash so consumers can parallelize. Precompute follower lists for high-fan-out accounts.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Separate queues per channel: failures in email delivery do not block push delivery; scaling is independent.

tipsAndTricks: Interview anchor: Use dedicated per-channel queues (push, email, SMS, in-app) to isolate delivery failures, apply hybrid write/read fanout at a follower-count threshold to avoid celebrity write amplification, and use Redis SETNX idempotency keys to deduplicate notifications without hitting the primary database.
Trade-off tip: Separate queues per channel: failures in email delivery do not block push delivery; scaling is independent.

Trade-off tip: Redis for preferences: avoids DB read on every notification event; stale preference cache (up to TTL) is acceptable — a user muting a notification type will stop receiving after the TTL expires.

Watch out for: Celebrity fanout: 5M push notifications in 5 seconds = 1M/sec. A single Kafka consumer + push worker cannot keep up. Solution: horizontal scaling of push workers; partition the notifications Kafka topic by userId hash so consumers can parallelize. Precompute follower lists for high-fan-out accounts.

Watch out for: APNs slow: push workers timeout waiting for APNs. Solution: set a short timeout (2 s); if APNs is slow, put undelivered notifications back in the queue with lower priority. Users will receive the push when APNs recovers.

putItTogether.title: Putting Design a Scalable Notification Service Together
putItTogether.summary: Use dedicated per-channel queues (push, email, SMS, in-app) to isolate delivery failures, apply hybrid write/read fanout at a follower-count threshold to avoid celebrity write amplification, and use Redis SETNX idempotency keys to deduplicate notifications without hitting the primary database.
steps: 1. Platform emits a domain event (e.g., UserLikedPost{postId, actorId, recipientId}) to Kafka.
2. Notification Service consumes the event: fetch recipient preferences from a low-latency cache (Redis); if the channel is disabled or event type is muted, drop the event.
3. Deduplication: check a Redis set {recipientId}:{eventType}:{entityId}:{windowHash} with TTL = dedup window (e.g., 1 hour). If key exists, drop; else SET NX and continue.
4. Batching worker: for low-priority types (likes, follows), accumulate events in a Redis sorted set by recipient, flush every 30 seconds, send a single batched notification.
putItTogether.outcome: Resilient end-to-end architecture ready for production spikes.
